result: The X5-Y-X5 library contains 1-10 million unique peptide sequences with 20% containing stop codons, and all 20 canonical amino acids are well-represented at each variable position.
evaluation: Claims C12-C14 are directly supported by deep sequencing analysis (C12, C13) and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 (C14). The library characterization is well-documented with appropriate sequencing depth and quality control metrics.

result: The X5-Y-X5 screen with c-Src recapitulates known sequence preferences (bulky aliphatic residues at -1, Phe at +3) and reveals additional preferences (+1 Asp/Glu/Ser), with no significant antibody bias.
evaluation: Claims C15-C20 are well-supported by screening data (Figures 1B, 1C) and comparison with prior literature (Deng et al., 2014; Songyang et al., 1995). The use of two different antibodies (C19) provides strong evidence against antibody bias (C20).

result: X5-Y-X5 screens reveal distinct sequence specificities for c-Abl, Fer, EPHB1, and EPHB2 kinases, with each showing characteristic position-specific amino acid preferences.
evaluation: Claims C21-C26 are supported by screening data in Figures 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The specificities are consistent with known preferences for c-Abl (C21-C23) and reveal novel patterns for Fer (C24) and EPH receptors (C25-C26).

result: Consensus peptides designed from X5-Y-X5 screens show high catalytic efficiency with their cognate kinases, though kinetic parameters differ from previously reported substrates and some peptides show cross-reactivity.
evaluation: Claims C27-C36 are supported by Michaelis-Menten analysis (Table 1) and kinetic assays (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The data demonstrate that consensus peptides are effective substrates but reveal trade-offs between kcat and KM (C27, C28, C33) and substrate overlap between kinases (C31, C32, C34-C36).

result: X5-Y-X5 screening data for c-Src correlates moderately with measured phosphorylation rates and accurately predicts the directionality of 5 out of 6 mutations.
evaluation: Claims C37-C38 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 3A) and mutational effect predictions (Figure 3B) using RP-HPLC validation. The moderate correlation (C37) and 83% accuracy in predicting mutational directionality (C38) demonstrate reasonable predictive power with acknowledged limitations.

result: The pTyr-Var library contains ~10,000 unique sequences spanning 3159 human phosphosites and 4760 disease-associated variants, with reproducible screening results across 3-5 replicates.
evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by library design documentation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and reproducibility analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3). The library composition is well-characterized and screens show good technical reproducibility.

result: The pTyr-Var screen with c-Src shows strong correlation with phosphorylation rates, consistent mutational effects with in vitro assays, and appropriate signal specificity with 7-10% of sequences showing enrichment above background.
evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are well-supported by correlation analysis (Figure 4B, 4C), negative controls (Figure 4A), and enrichment distribution (Figure 4—figure supplement 4). The strong correlation for high-activity sequences (C42) and consistency with orthogonal assays (C43) validate the screening approach.

result: pTyr-Var screens reveal correlation patterns between kinase families and show that 30-40% of literature-reported kinase-substrate pairs are efficiently phosphorylated in the screen.
evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 4D) and comparison with PhosphoSitePlus database (Figure 4—source data 1). The family-specific correlations (C46-C48) are expected, and the 30-40% overlap with literature (C49) is reasonable given the limitations of peptide-based assays.

result: pTyr-Var screens identify hundreds of high-confidence phosphosite-proximal mutations with kinase-specific patterns, including the RET R982C mutation that enhances phosphorylation by c-Src and Fer.
evaluation: Claims C50-C53 are supported by filtering analysis (Figure 4E), position-specific sensitivity patterns (Figure 4—figure supplement 7), and specific examples (Figure 4—figure supplement 8). The identification of 381 mutations for c-Src (C50) with distinct positional patterns (C51) demonstrates the screen's ability to detect functionally relevant variants.

result: SHP2 Tyr 62 is preferentially phosphorylated by receptor tyrosine kinases over non-receptors, and D61 mutations show kinase-specific effects in screens that are validated by intact protein mass spectrometry.
evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by screening data (Figure 4—figure supplement 9) and intact protein mass spectrometry validation (Figure 4F). The kinase-specific effects of D61V and D61N mutations observed in screens (C55) are confirmed in the context of full-length protein (C57, C58), though both mutations enhance phosphorylation more than predicted from peptide screens (C57).

result: Position-specific scoring matrices from X5-Y-X5 screens show modest correlation with pTyr-Var data, with many context-dependent effects where mutations have different impacts depending on sequence context.
evaluation: Claims C59-C64 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), rate measurements (Figure 5B-D), and mutational effect comparisons (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2). The identification of context-dependent effects (C61-C63) and 5-15% of mutations with opposite effects (C64) demonstrates limitations of position-specific scoring matrices.

result: X5-Y-X5 screens with c-Src, SHP2-C, and Grb2 SH2 domains recapitulate known sequence preferences and reveal subtle additional preferences.
evaluation: Claims C65-C69 are supported by screening data (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 3) and comparison with literature. The preferences for c-Src SH2 (C66), Grb2 (C67), and SHP2-C (C69) match known specificities, with additional subtle preferences revealed (C68).

result: pTyr-Var screens with SH2 domains show high reproducibility, distinct specificities between domains, and good correlation with measured binding affinities over two orders of magnitude.
evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 4), enrichment distributions (Figure 6C), and binding affinity validation (Figure 6D). The strong correlation between enrichment scores and Kd values (C73) validates the screening approach for SH2 domains.

result: pTyr-Var screens identify 50-300 phosphosite-proximal mutations affecting SH2 binding with domain-specific patterns, and reveal orthogonal specificities between c-Src kinase and SH2 domains.
evaluation: Claims C74-C78 are supported by filtering analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 5, 6), comparison of kinase and SH2 profiles (Figure 6—figure supplement 7, 8), and mechanistic interpretation. The orthogonal specificities (C76) attributed to +3 position preferences (C77) provide mechanistic insight into c-Src regulation.

result: Amber suppression successfully incorporates non-canonical amino acids (CMF and AzF) into the X5-Y-X5 library, as confirmed by flow cytometry and click chemistry labeling.
evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are supported by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 7B, 7C) showing increased peptide display with CMF (C80) and specific DIBO labeling with AzF (C81). The controls (without synthetase or without non-canonical amino acid) are appropriate.

result: CMF is enriched at -3 and -2 positions where Phe is not tolerated by c-Src, potentially mimicking negatively-charged amino acids, and is depleted at the +3 position.
evaluation: Claims C82 and C84 are directly supported by screening data (Figure 7D). Claim C83 is a reasonable mechanistic interpretation based on the chemical properties of CMF and observed enrichment patterns, though it remains speculative without direct structural evidence.

result: Lysine is unfavorable for c-Src at all positions, but acetylation (AcK) is tolerated or favorable at several positions, with similar patterns across c-Src, Hck, and c-Abl, and up to 5-10-fold enhancement at the +1 position.
evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are supported by screening data (Figure 7D) and in vitro kinetic validation (Figure 7—figure supplement 3). The position-dependent tolerance for AcK over Lys (C86, C87) and quantitative enhancement at +1 position (C88) demonstrate the functional impact of lysine acetylation on kinase recognition.

result: The bacterial peptide display platform provides an accessible, high-throughput method for profiling phosphotyrosine signaling proteins, with data showing strong correlation to orthogonal biochemical assays.
evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by the collective evidence from the study. The accessibility (C90, C91) is demonstrated by the benchtop magnetic bead approach, and strong correlations with orthogonal assays (C92) are shown in Figures 3, 4, and 6.

result: Background claims establish that tyrosine phosphorylation is essential in metazoans, that kinases and SH2 domains discriminate among phosphosites based on sequence context, and that oriented peptide libraries have been used to characterize kinome specificity.
evaluation: Claims C1-C11 are background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims provide context for the current work and are not primary findings of this study.

result: The platform will augment computational approaches, provide opportunities to investigate variant effects, and can be adapted to other protein modification systems including phosphatases, deacetylases, and serine/threonine kinases.
evaluation: Claims C93-C101 are primarily speculative statements about future applications and potential uses of the platform. While reasonable based on the demonstrated capabilities, these represent proposed future work rather than validated results from the current study.
